messages.content: How many stars are in our galaxy?

function.name: requests_get
function.description: Sends a GET request to the specified URL and retrieves data as specified by the parameters. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

url.description: The URL to which the GET request is sent. It is expected to be a well-formed HTTP or HTTPS URL.

Content-Type.description: The MIME type of the body of the request (used with POST and PUT requests).

Accept.description: The Media type(s) that is/are acceptable for the response.

headers.description: A dictionary of HTTP headers to send with the request. Each key-value pair represents a header name and its value.

timeout.description: The number of seconds to wait for the server to send data before giving up, as a float, or a (connect_timeout, read_timeout) tuple. This is a float type value.

lat.description: Latitude of the location for the query, in degrees. This is a float type value.

lon.description: Longitude of the location for the query, in degrees. This is a float type value.

params.description: Query parameters to append to the URL for the GET request.

allow_redirects.description: Determines if HTTP redirections (301, 302, etc.) should be followed.

auth.description: A tuple representing the user credentials for HTTP authentication, typically in the form of (username, password).

cert.description: Path to an SSL certificate file to verify the peer, or a tuple of (certificate file, key file).

cookies.description: A dictionary of cookies to send with the request. The key is the cookie name and the value is the cookie value.

http.description: URL of the proxy for HTTP requests.

https.description: URL of the proxy for HTTPS requests.

proxies.description: A dictionary mapping protocol names to the URL of the proxy.

stream.description: If True, the response content will not be downloaded immediately but streamed.

verify.description: Whether to verify the server's TLS certificate or not, or a path to a CA bundle if verification is needed.

message.content:
**Answer**

Astronomers estimate that the Milky Way contains roughly **200 billion to 400 billion stars** – i.e., between \(2\times10^{11}\) and \(4\times10^{11}\).

---

### Why the range?

| Factor | Effect |
|--------|-------|
| **Stellar census limits** | Most surveys miss very dim M‑dwarfs and substellar objects because they emit little visible light. Adding those increases the total. |
| **Uncertainty in Galactic mass** | Dynamical models infer stellar masses from rotation curves; small changes in assumed dark matter distribution shift the inferred luminous mass. |
| **Recent Gaia data** | The European Space Agency’s *Gaia* satellite has mapped over a billion stars with unprecedented precision. Early releases suggest ≈\(2.7 \times 10^9\) bright stars within 20 kpc, implying a full population when extrapolated. |

> **Key reference:**  
> - *Bovy & Rix (2013)* “Mapping the Galaxy” – gives a robust dynamical estimate of \(M_{\star,\text{MW}}\approx(5\pm1)\times10^{10}\,M_\odot\), corresponding to ∼\(2–4\times10^{11}\) main‑sequence stars assuming a Kroupa IMF.  

---

#### Quick sanity check

If you take the average luminosity of a Sun‑like G‑type star (\(\sim L_\odot\)) and assume the Milky Way radiates at about \(L_{\rm MW}\approx 2\times10^{10}\,L_\odot\) (from integrated infrared measurements), then:

\[
N_{\ast}\;\approx\;\frac{L_{\rm MW}}{\langle L\rangle}
          \;\approx\;
          \frac{2\times10^{10}\,L_\odot}{1\,L_\odot}
          \;\approx\;2\times10^{10}.
\]

That simple back‑of‑the‑nap calculation underestimates the real figure because it ignores the far more numerous lower‑mass stars (< 0.5 \(M_\odot\)). When their contribution is added—using standard initial mass functions—the tally climbs into the few‑hundred‑billions range.

---

### Bottom line

While there isn’t a single definitive number, the consensus among modern galactic astronomers places the Milky Way’s stellar inventory somewhere between **200 and 400 billion stars**. Future deep‑infrared missions (e.g., JWST, Roman Telescope) may refine this further by detecting even fainter members of the disk and halo populations.
